text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Severe symptomatic anemia\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Acute bleeding\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Myocardial ischemia\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Which blood product?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">NOT whole blood.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Caution in CKD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Transfusion may cause:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">because stored blood leaks potassium.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This was asked by:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dr. Bell and Dr. Nyasatu.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Other complications\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Iron overload   •  Volume overload   •  Alloimmunization   •  Difficulty finding transplant donor later\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">VIVA QUESTIONS\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 36\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q1.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is anemia common in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Answer\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because damaged kidneys fail to produce adequate erythropoietin, resulting in reduced red blood\u003cbr>cell production. Other contributing factors include iron deficiency, inflammation, shortened RBC\u003cbr>survival, and uremic bone marrow suppression.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q2.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">What type of anemia occurs in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normocytic\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Normochromic\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q3.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hb is 9 g/dL and ferritin is normal.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Will you transfuse?\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">NO.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Give:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Erythropoietin.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q4.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target Hb in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10–11.5 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Not normal.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q5.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why can repeated transfusions be harmful?\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 37\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because they may cause:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hyperkalemia   •  Iron overload   •  Alloimmunization   •  Volume overload\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CKD COMPLICATION 2\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE–MINERAL AND BONE DISORDER (CKD-MBD)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD) is a systemic disorder of mineral metabolism that\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">develops as kidney function progressively declines. It is characterized by abnormalities in\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and vitamin D metabolism, resulting in bone\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">disease, vascular calcification, and increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. CKD-MBD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">usually begins early in CKD, often from stage 3 onward, and becomes increasingly severe as\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">patients approach end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The importance of CKD-MBD extends beyond bones. Although patients may present with bone\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">pain or fractures, the major cause of death associated with CKD-MBD is actually cardiovascular\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">disease due to calcification of blood vessels and heart valves. Therefore, understanding this\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">complication is essential for both examinations and clinical practice.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">NORMAL PHYSIOLOGY OF CALCIUM AND PHOSPHATE\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Under normal circumstances, the kidneys play a central role in maintaining calcium and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">phosphate balance. Dietary calcium and phosphate are absorbed in the intestines under the\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">influence of calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D. The kidneys excrete excess phosphate and\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 38\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">convert inactive vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D) into calcitriol through the enzyme 1-alpha\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hydroxylase.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcitriol increases intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate. When serum calcium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">falls, the parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which restores calcium levels\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">by increasing bone resorption, enhancing renal calcium reabsorption, and stimulating calcitriol\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">production.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This delicate balance becomes disrupted in CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CKD-MBD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The earliest abnormality in CKD-MBD is phosphate retention.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As the glomerular filtration rate declines, the kidneys lose their ability to excrete phosphate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">efficiently. Initially, serum phosphate may remain normal because compensatory hormones such\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">as fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF-23) and parathyroid hormone increase phosphate excretion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">by the remaining nephrons. However, as CKD progresses, these compensatory mechanisms\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">become inadequate, and phosphate begins to accumulate in the blood, leading to\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hyperphosphatemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">At the same time, the diseased kidneys lose the ability to activate vitamin D because the enzyme\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1-alpha hydroxylase becomes deficient. Consequently, levels of calcitriol fall. Since calcitriol is\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">necessary for intestinal calcium absorption, patients develop reduced calcium absorption from\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">the gut, resulting in hypocalcemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The combination of:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hyperphosphatemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Reduced calcitriol\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">stimulates the parathyroid glands to secrete increasing amounts of PTH. Initially this response is\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">beneficial because PTH mobilizes calcium from bone and increases phosphate excretion.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 39\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, persistent stimulation causes enlargement of the parathyroid glands and chronic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">elevation of PTH, a condition known as secondary hyperparathyroidism.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Persistently elevated PTH causes excessive bone turnover and resorption. Bone becomes weak,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">painful, and susceptible to fractures. This skeletal manifestation is called renal osteodystrophy,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">which represents the bone component of CKD-MBD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Meanwhile, excess calcium and phosphate precipitate in blood vessels and soft tissues, causing\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">vascular calcification. Coronary artery calcification, calcification of heart valves, and arterial\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">stiffness are major contributors to cardiovascular mortality in CKD patients.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Summary\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Reduced GFR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Reduced phosphate excretion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperphosphatemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Reduced 1-alpha hydroxylase activity\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Reduced calcitriol\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 40\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Reduced intestinal calcium absorption\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Increased PTH secretion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Secondary hyperparathyroidism\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Renal osteodystrophy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">WHY IS PTH ELEVATED IN CKD?\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is one of the most commonly asked viva questions.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PTH rises because:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. The kidneys cannot excrete phosphate → phosphate accumulates.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Diseased kidneys produce less calcitriol.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Reduced calcitriol causes decreased intestinal calcium absorption.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Serum calcium falls.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. The parathyroid glands sense hypocalcemia and increase PTH secretion.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. Chronic stimulation causes secondary hyperparathyroidism.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">TYPES OF RENAL OSTEODYSTROPHY\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 41\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Renal osteodystrophy refers to the skeletal abnormalities associated with CKD-MBD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The major types are:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Osteitis Fibrosa Cystica\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is the most common type and is caused by secondary hyperparathyroidism.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Excess PTH stimulates osteoclast activity, causing:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone resorption\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone pain\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fractures\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Subperiosteal bone erosion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Brown tumors\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Osteomalacia\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Osteomalacia results from defective bone mineralization.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vitamin D deficiency\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Aluminum toxicity (rare nowadays)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone pain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Muscle weakness\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fractures\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Adynamic Bone Disease\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is characterized by markedly reduced bone turnover.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It occurs when PTH is excessively suppressed, usually due to:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 42\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Excessive calcium supplementation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Excessive vitamin D therapy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Over-treatment with calcimimetics\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients have:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fragile bones\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fractures\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Mixed Uremic Osteodystrophy\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Features of both:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  High bone turnover\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Defective mineralization\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CLINICAL FEATURES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients may initially be asymptomatic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As disease progresses, they may develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Skeletal manifestations\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone pain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Muscle weakness\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fractures\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Rib pain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Difficulty walking\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Skeletal deformities\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Soft tissue manifestations\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Pruritus\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 43\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Tendon rupture\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Calciphylaxis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cardiovascular manifestation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Coronary artery calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Aortic valve calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Mitral valve calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Arterial stiffness\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Heart failure\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CALCIPHYLAXIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calciphylaxis is a rare but severe complication.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It occurs due to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium-phosphate deposition\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Small vessel calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Ischemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Skin necrosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Painful skin lesions\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Purple plaques\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Necrotic ulcers\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 44\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mortality is extremely high because of sepsis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIAGNOSIS OF CKD-MBD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis requires a combination of laboratory investigations and imaging.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Blood Tests\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Serum Calcium\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Low\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">because calcitriol production is reduced.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Serum Phosphate\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">High\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">because the kidneys cannot excrete phosphate.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Elevated\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">especially in advanced CKD.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Vitamin D\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcitriol:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Low\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 45\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May be elevated in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Osteitis fibrosa cystica\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  High bone turnover states\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Imaging\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">X-rays\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May show:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Subperiosteal bone resorption\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone cysts\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Osteopenia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Brown tumors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">DEXA scan\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Measures:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Bone mineral density.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Echocardiography\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May demonstrate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Aortic valve calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Mitral valve calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CT scan\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Can assess:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Coronary artery calcification\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 46\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT OF CKD-MBD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Treatment aims to:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Reduce phosphate.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Correct vitamin D deficiency.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Control PTH.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Prevent fractures and vascular calcification.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. PHOSPHATE RESTRICTION\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients should reduce intake of:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Milk\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Cheese\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Yogurt\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Red meat\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Soft drinks\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Processed foods\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Nuts\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dietary counseling by a renal dietitian is very important.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. PHOSPHATE BINDERS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Phosphate binders prevent intestinal phosphate absorption.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium Carbonate\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">500–1500 mg\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 47\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Three times daily.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why should calcium carbonate be taken WITH meals?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a favorite viva question.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium carbonate acts as a phosphate binder.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It binds dietary phosphate inside the gastrointestinal tract before phosphate can be absorbed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Take calcium carbonate WITH meals.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If taken on an empty stomach, its phosphate-binding effect is significantly reduced.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypercalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Constipation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Nephrolithiasis\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Sevelamer\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sevelamer is a non-calcium phosphate binder.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">800–1600 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Three times daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">WITH meals.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Advantages\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 48\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  No hypercalcemia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Reduces LDL cholesterol\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Less vascular calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bloating\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Nausea\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Constipation\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. CALCITRIOL\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is given to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Increase calcium absorption\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Suppress PTH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Treat secondary hyperparathyroidism\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">0.25–1 mcg daily\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypercalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hyperphosphatemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. CINACALCET\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It increases the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid gland.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As a result:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 49\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PTH secretion decreases.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">30 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Can increase to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">60 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">90 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">120 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">according to PTH levels.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Nausea\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vomiting\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. PARATHYROIDECTOMY\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Indications:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe secondary hyperparathyroidism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Persistent PTH elevation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone pain\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fractures\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Calciphylaxis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Failure of medical treatment\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 50\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">VIVA QUESTIONS\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q1.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is phosphate elevated in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because declining GFR reduces phosphate excretion, causing phosphate retention.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q2.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is calcium low?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because diseased kidneys cannot produce calcitriol, reducing intestinal calcium absorption.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q3.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is PTH elevated?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia stimulate the parathyroid glands, causing secondary\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">hyperparathyroidism.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q4.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is calcium carbonate given WITH meals?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because it binds dietary phosphate inside the intestine and prevents its absorption.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q5.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">What are the types of renal osteodystrophy?\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Osteitis fibrosa cystica\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Osteomalacia\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Adynamic bone disease\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Mixed uremic osteodystrophy\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 51\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q6.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">What kills CKD-MBD patients most often?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cardiovascular disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">due to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Coronary artery calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Valvular calcification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Vascular stiffness\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EXAM PEARL\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Remember:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD-MBD is NOT only a bone disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is a systemic disorder involving:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Bone\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Blood vessels\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Heart valves\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Soft tissues\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Parathyroid glands\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and cardiovascular complications are the leading cause of death.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CKD COMPLICATION 3\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia is one of the most important and feared complications of chronic kidney disease. It refers\u003cbr>to the clinical syndrome that results from the accumulation of toxic substances normally\u003cbr>excreted by the kidneys. Although many people use the terms uremia and azotemia\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 52\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">interchangeably, they are not exactly the same. Azotemia simply means elevated blood levels of\u003cbr>nitrogenous waste products such as urea and creatinine, whereas uremia refers to the\u003cbr>constellation of signs and symptoms caused by these toxins. In other words, a patient can have\u003cbr>azotemia without symptoms, but once the toxins begin to affect multiple organ systems, the\u003cbr>patient is said to have uremia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia usually develops in advanced CKD, particularly when the eGFR falls below 15\u003cbr>mL/min/1.73 m² (CKD stage 5), although symptoms may appear earlier depending on the rate of\u003cbr>progression and associated illnesses.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF UREMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The kidneys normally excrete thousands of metabolic waste products. In CKD, declining GFR\u003cbr>leads to retention of these substances, collectively called uremic toxins. These toxins are\u003cbr>chemically diverse and include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Urea\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Creatinine\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Guanidines\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Phenols\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Indoles\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Middle molecules (e.g., β2-microglobulin)\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Advanced glycation end products\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Inflammatory cytokines\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These substances are toxic to virtually every organ system. They interfere with\u003cbr>neurotransmission, platelet function, gastric mucosal integrity, cardiac function, immune\u003cbr>responses, and endocrine pathways. Consequently, uremia is not a single disease but rather a\u003cbr>multisystem disorder.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">SYSTEMIC MANIFESTATIONS OF UREMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Central nervous system\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins cross the blood-brain barrier and alter neuronal function. Patients initially  develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fatigue   •  Poor concentration   •  Sleep disturbances   •  Memory impairment\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As toxin levels rise:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Confusion   •  Disorientation\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 53\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Asterixis   •  Delirium   •  Seizures   •  Coma\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This condition is called:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC ENCEPHALOPATHY\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Gastrointestinal system\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins irritate the gastric and intestinal mucosa and stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger  zone.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Anorexia   •  Nausea   •  Vomiting   •  Metallic taste   •  Weight loss   •  Hiccups\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This condition is known as:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC GASTRITIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Cardiovascular system\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia can cause:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Pericarditis   •  Cardiomyopathy   •  Arrhythmias   •  Accelerated atherosclerosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hematological system\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Platelet dysfunction   •  Bleeding tendency   •  Easy bruising   •  Epistaxis   •  GI bleeding\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 54\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Skin\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients may have:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Severe pruritus   •  Xerosis   •  Hyperpigmentation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In very severe cases:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic frost\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">which occurs when urea crystals deposit on the skin surface after sweating.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC ENCEPHALOPATHY\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pathophysiology\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic encephalopathy occurs because uremic toxins accumulate in the brain and interfere with\u003cbr>neurotransmission, neuronal metabolism, and cerebral blood flow.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The exact mechanisms are not fully understood, but several factors contribute:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Accumulation of neurotoxins\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Compounds such as guanidines, parathyroid hormone fragments, and inflammatory mediators\u003cbr>accumulate in CKD and impair neuronal signaling.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Metabolic acidosis\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD patients are unable to excrete hydrogen ions.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Alters neuronal excitability   •  Depresses CNS function\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Electrolyte disturbances\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Especially:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hypernatremia   •  Hyponatremia   •  Hypercalcemia   •  Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 55\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These abnormalities worsen neurological dysfunction.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Secondary hyperparathyroidism\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">High PTH levels may have neurotoxic effects.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Features\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Early:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fatigue   •  Difficulty concentrating   •  Irritability   •  Sleep disturbance\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Moderate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Confusion   •  Disorientation   •  Memory loss   •  Tremors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Asterixis   •  Seizures   •  Delirium   •  Coma\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Physical Examination\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">You may find:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Asterixis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask the patient to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Extend arms   •  Dorsiflex wrists\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">There will be:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Flapping tremor.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperreflexia may be present.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 56\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In severe disease:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Stupor   •  Coma\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis is clinical.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Supportive findings include:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Elevated\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Urea   •  Creatinine\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Low:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Serum bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Electrolyte abnormalities\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hyperkalemia   •  Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EEG\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May show:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Generalized slowing\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CT brain\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually normal.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Done to exclude:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Stroke   •  Tumor   •  Hemorrhage\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DEFINITIVE TREATMENT\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 57\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIALYSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is the treatment of choice.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis removes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Uremic toxins   •  Excess potassium   •  Excess fluid\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Supportive treatment\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Correct:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Acidosis   •  Hyperkalemia   •  Hypocalcemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Treat:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Infection   •  Hypertension\u003c/h4>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Important Viva Question\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Will bicarbonate cure uremic encephalopathy?\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">NO.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It may improve acidosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The definitive treatment is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC GASTRITIS\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pathophysiology\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic gastritis occurs because retained uremic toxins irritate the gastrointestinal mucosa.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Several mechanisms contribute:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Direct mucosal irritation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 58\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Damage gastric epithelium   •  Increase inflammation\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Increased gastrin\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The kidneys normally help metabolize gastrin.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In CKD:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Gastrin accumulates\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Increased acid secretion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mucosal injury.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Platelet dysfunction\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">CKD patients have impaired platelet aggregation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Small erosions\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Can bleed significantly.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Delayed gastric emptying\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia impairs autonomic function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Early satiety   •  Nausea   •  Vomiting\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Features\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients may present with:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 59\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Nausea   •  Vomiting   •  Metallic taste   •  Anorexia   •  Epigastric pain   •  Weight loss\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe disease:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hematemesis   •  Melena   •  GI bleeding\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CBC\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May show:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Anemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urea and Creatinine\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually elevated.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">May reveal:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Gastritis   •  Gastric erosions   •  Ulcers   •  Bleeding lesions\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Proton Pump Inhibitors\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Omeprazole\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">20–40 mg OD.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pantoprazole\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 60\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">40 mg OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">or\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">40 mg IV BD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">if bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side Effects of PPIs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Headache   •  Diarrhea   •  Vitamin B12 deficiency   •  Increased risk of C. difficile infection\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Antiemetics\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Metoclopramide\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 mg TDS.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Ondansetron\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">4–8 mg.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Dialysis\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Definitive treatment.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Why?\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Because dialysis removes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC BLEEDING TENDENCY\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is another favorite viva topic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why do CKD patients bleed?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The problem is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelet dysfunction\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">NOT thrombocytopenia.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 61\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pathophysiology\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins impair:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelet adhesion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelets cannot attach properly to damaged endothelium.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelet aggregation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelets cannot bind effectively to each other.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelet degranulation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelets release less:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  ADP   •  Serotonin   •  Thromboxane\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">which are important for clot formation.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Result\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The patient bleeds easily despite:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Normal platelet count   •  Normal PT   •  Normal INR\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical Features\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Easy bruising\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Epistaxis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Gingival bleeding\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>GI bleeding\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Menorrhagia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Prolonged bleeding after procedures\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis\u003c/h4>\u003ch3 Dialysis\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Best treatment.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis removes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremic toxins\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and improves platelet function.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. DDAVP (Desmopressin)\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Very important viva.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Increases release of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Factor VIII   •  Von Willebrand factor\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">0.3 mcg/kg IV\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">before:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Surgery   •  Biopsy   •  Invasive procedures\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Cryoprecipitate\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 63\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Contains:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Factor VIII   •  Fibrinogen   •  vWF\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Used if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UREMIC FROST\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a classic exam picture.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It occurs in:\u003c/p>\u003cp form on skin.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Looks like:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Frost\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">or\u003c/p>\u003cp 64\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The frost disappears after dialysis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EXAM class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical syndrome caused by accumulation of uremic toxins.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q2.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">What causes bleeding in CKD?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Platelet dysfunction.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Not thrombocytopenia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">Q3.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patient has CKD with confusion and asterixis.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definitive treatment of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Uremic encephalopathy?   •  Uremic gastritis?   •  Uremic bleeding?\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 65\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIALYSIS.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EXAM PEARL\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Remember:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Uremia affects EVERY organ system.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Think:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Brain → Encephalopathy\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Stomach → Gastritis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Heart → Pericarditis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Platelets → Bleeding\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Skin → Pruritus and frost\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">and the definitive treatment for severe symptomatic uremia is usually:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CKD COMPLICATION 4\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ELECTROLYTE ABNORMALITIES AND ACID–BASE DISORDERS IN CKD\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Electrolyte and acid-base disturbances are among the most dangerous complications of chronic\u003cbr>kidney disease. The kidneys are responsible for maintaining homeostasis by regulating sodium,\u003cbr>potassium, hydrogen ions, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, and water. As kidney function\u003cbr>declines, this regulatory capacity progressively deteriorates. Consequently, patients with\u003cbr>advanced CKD develop abnormalities that can affect almost every organ system, particularly the\u003cbr>heart, nervous system, muscles, and bones.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Among these abnormalities, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis are especially important\u003cbr>because they can become life-threatening and are common indications for emergency dialysis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. HYPERKALEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia is one of the most feared complications of CKD because it can cause fatal cardiac\u003cbr>arrhythmias. Potassium is predominantly an intracellular ion, and the kidneys are responsible for\u003cbr>excreting approximately 90–95% of the daily potassium load. In CKD, the number of\u003cbr>functioning nephrons decreases progressively. Initially, the remaining nephrons compensate by\u003cbr>increasing potassium secretion. However, as GFR falls below approximately 20–30 mL/min/1.73\u003cbr>m², this compensatory mechanism becomes inadequate and potassium begins to accumulate in\u003cbr>the bloodstream.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 66\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia may be worsened by medications commonly prescribed in CKD, such as ACE\u003cbr>inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, and NSAIDs. Conditions such as metabolic acidosis, tissue\u003cbr>breakdown, or excessive dietary potassium intake can further increase serum potassium levels.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF HYPERKALEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normally, potassium excretion occurs mainly in the distal nephron under the influence of\u003cbr>aldosterone. Aldosterone stimulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. In CKD,\u003cbr>several factors impair this process:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Reduced nephron mass means fewer tubules are available for potassium excretion.\u003cbr>2. Reduced distal tubular flow limits potassium secretion.\u003cbr>3. Many CKD patients have impaired RAAS activity or are taking ACE inhibitors and\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ARBs, which reduce aldosterone levels.\u003cbr>4. Metabolic acidosis promotes movement of potassium from the intracellular compartment\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">to the extracellular space.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As potassium accumulates, the resting membrane potential of cardiac myocytes becomes less\u003cbr>negative. Initially this increases myocardial excitability, but severe hyperkalemia eventually\u003cbr>suppresses cardiac conduction and can precipitate ventricular fibrillation or asystole.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CLINICAL FEATURES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mild hyperkalemia may be asymptomatic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As potassium rises, patients may develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Generalized weakness  •  Fatigue  •  Paresthesia  •  Muscle cramps  •  Flaccid paralysis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe hyperkalemia may present with:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Palpitations  •  Syncope  •  Ventricular arrhythmias  •  Cardiac arrest\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ECG CHANGES IN HYPERKALEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ECG findings correlate approximately with serum potassium levels.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium 5.5–6.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 67\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">You may see:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tall, peaked T waves\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These are classically narrow-based and symmetrical.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium 6.5–7.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Prolonged PR interval  •  Flattened P waves\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium 7.5–8.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Wide QRS complexes  •  Disappearance of P waves\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium &gt;8.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sine wave pattern\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a pre-terminal rhythm.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Progression may occur to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Ventricular fibrillation  •  Asystole\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">EXAM PEARL\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Any CKD patient with hyperkalemia requires an ECG immediately.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If ECG changes are present:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is a medical emergency.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIAGNOSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum potassium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">3.5–5.0 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&gt;5.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 68\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Severe hyperkalemia:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">≥6.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Any ECG changes.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ECG\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Peaked T waves  •  Wide QRS  •  Flattened P waves  •  Sine wave\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT OF HYPERKALEMIA\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management is based on three principles:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Stabilize the myocardium.  2. Shift potassium into cells.  3. Remove potassium from the body.\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">STEP 1\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Stabilize the myocardium\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium gluconate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10%\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 mL IV\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Over:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">2–5 minutes.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Calcium does NOT lower potassium.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It stabilizes the cardiac membrane and reduces the risk of arrhythmia.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 69\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Onset\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1–3 minutes.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Duration\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">30–60 minutes.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">STEP 2\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Shift potassium intracellularly\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Insulin + Dextrose\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Regular insulin:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10 units IV\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PLUS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">25 g dextrose\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">(50 mL of 50% dextrose)\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Insulin activates:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Na+/K+ ATPase\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">which moves potassium into cells.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Onset\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">15–30 min\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Duration\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">4–6 hours\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effect\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hypoglycemia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Monitor glucose.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 70\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Salbutamol\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Nebulized:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">10–20 mg\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Stimulates β2 receptors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Activates Na+/K+ ATPase\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Moves potassium into cells.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Tremor  •  Tachycardia\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sodium bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Useful if:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis is present.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">50–100 mmol IV\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">STEP 3\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Remove potassium from the body\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Loop diuretics\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Furosemide\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">40–80 mg IV\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 71\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">if urine output is preserved.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Potassium binders\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate  •  Patiromer\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIALYSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is the definitive treatment.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Indications\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hyperkalemia:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">K &gt;6.5 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ECG changes\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">OR\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Failure of medical therapy.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. METABOLIC ACIDOSIS\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis is another common complication of CKD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The kidneys normally:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Reabsorb bicarbonate.  •  Excrete hydrogen ions.  •  Generate new bicarbonate.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">As kidney function declines, these processes become impaired. Hydrogen ions accumulate while\u003cbr>bicarbonate levels fall, producing chronic metabolic acidosis.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">PATHOPHYSIOLOGY\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal metabolism produces acids every day.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examples:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 72\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Sulfuric acid  •  Phosphoric acid  •  Organic acids\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Healthy kidneys excrete these acids and regenerate bicarbonate.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In CKD:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hydrogen ion excretion decreases.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acid accumulates.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Bicarbonate is consumed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum bicarbonate falls.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Metabolic acidosis develops.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Why is metabolic acidosis harmful?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acidosis:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Stimulates muscle breakdown\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Promotes bone demineralization\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Increases inflammation\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Worsens hyperkalemia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Accelerates CKD progression\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CLINICAL FEATURES\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients may develop:\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fatigue  •  Weakness  •  Nausea  •  Dyspnea\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 73\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Kussmaul breathing  •  Confusion\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">DIAGNOSIS\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ABG\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">You will find:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Low pH\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;7.35\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Low bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;22 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Compensation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">↓\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PaCO₂\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">because of hyperventilation.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">MANAGEMENT\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sodium bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Indication:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum bicarbonate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">&lt;22 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Dose:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">650–1300 mg\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">BD–TDS.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Target:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Serum bicarbonate:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 74\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">22–26 mmol/L\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fluid overload  •  Hypertension  •  Edema\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Dialysis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Indicated if:\u003c/p>\u003cp
