chronic kidney disease (ckd) definition chronic kidney disease (ckd) is a progressive and irreversible loss of kidney function characterized by abnormalities in kidney structure or function that persist for at least three months and have implications for health. according to the kdigo guidelines, ckd is diagnosed when there is either a reduction in the glomerular filtration rate (gfr) to less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m² for more than three months or evidence of kidney damage regardless of gfr. evidence of kidney damage may include albuminuria, abnormalities in urine sediment, electrolyte disturbances due to tubular disorders, structural abnormalities detected by imaging, or histological abnormalities on kidney biopsy. ckd is an important global health problem because it increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, hospitalization, kidney failure, and premature death. must know kdigo criteria for ckd ckd is present if either of the following persists for ≥3 months: 1. gfr \u003c60 ml/min/1.73m² 2. evidence of kidney damage: o albuminuria (acr ≥30 mg/g) o urine sediment abnormalities o electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders o histological abnormalities o structural abnormalities on imaging o history of kidney transplantation normal kidney physiology before understanding ckd, one must first understand how the kidneys normally function. the kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs responsible for maintaining the internal environment of the body. they regulate water balance, electrolyte concentrations, acid-base status, blood pressure, erythropoiesis, and bone metabolism. each kidney contains approximately one million nephrons, which are the functional units responsible for filtering blood and forming urine. a nephron consists of the glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct. the glomerulus acts as a highly specialized filtration barrier. blood enters through the afferent arteriole and leaves via the efferent arteriole. filtration occurs across three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocytes. water and small solutes pass through this barrier into bowman's capsule, while large proteins and blood cells are retained within the circulation. the amount of filtrate formed per minute is called the glomerular filtration rate (gfr), which normally ranges from approximately 90–120 ml/min/1.73 m² in healthy adults. after filtration, the renal tubules modify the filtrate extensively. the proximal tubule reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids, and most sodium and bicarbonate. the loop of henle establishes the concentration gradient necessary for urine concentration. the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct are regulated by hormones such as aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (adh), allowing fine adjustment of sodium and water balance. in addition to filtration and excretion, the kidneys perform important endocrine functions. specialized interstitial cells produce erythropoietin (epo), which stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. the kidneys also convert inactive vitamin d into its active form, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin d), which is essential for calcium absorption and bone health. furthermore, the kidneys participate in blood pressure regulation through the renin-angiotensin- aldosterone system (raas). any chronic injury to the kidneys disrupts these functions and leads to the diverse manifestations observed in ckd. must know major functions of the kidney 1. excretion of waste products o urea o creatinine o uric acid o drugs and toxins 2. regulation of: o water balance o sodium o potassium o calcium o phosphate o acid-base balance 3. endocrine functions: o erythropoietin production o vitamin d activation o renin secretion etiology of ckd chronic kidney disease is not a single disease but rather a syndrome resulting from many different disorders that cause progressive nephron destruction. the prevalence of specific causes varies by region. in developed countries, diabetes mellitus and hypertension account for the majority of cases. in sub-saharan africa, however, hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, hiv-associated nephropathy, and obstructive uropathy remain major contributors. diabetes mellitus diabetes mellitus is currently the leading cause of ckd worldwide. chronic hyperglycemia causes glycation of proteins within the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium. this results in thickening of the basement membrane, mesangial expansion, podocyte injury, and glomerulosclerosis. initially, diabetic patients develop hyperfiltration and microalbuminuria. over time, persistent proteinuria and fibrosis lead to progressive decline in renal function. hypertension hypertension damages the small arteries and arterioles supplying the kidneys. persistent high pressure causes hyaline arteriosclerosis, narrowing of blood vessels, and ischemic injury to nephrons. the glomeruli gradually become sclerotic, and the kidneys shrink in size. hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of ckd, creating a vicious cycle that accelerates disease progression. chronic glomerulonephritis glomerulonephritis encompasses a group of immune-mediated diseases affecting the glomeruli. persistent inflammation results in glomerular destruction and fibrosis. patients may initially present with hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, or nephrotic syndrome before progressing to ckd. obstructive uropathy long-standing obstruction of urine flow, such as from benign prostatic hyperplasia (bph), prostate cancer, ureteric stones, or strictures, causes back pressure on the kidneys. persistent obstruction leads to hydronephrosis, tubular atrophy, and irreversible nephron loss. hiv-associated nephropathy (hivan) hiv can directly infect renal epithelial cells, leading to collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (fsgs). patients often present with nephrotic-range proteinuria and rapidly progressive renal failure. unlike many other causes of ckd, hivan often produces enlarged kidneys on ultrasound. pathophysiology the progression of chronic kidney disease is not simply a consequence of the initial kidney injury but is largely driven by maladaptive responses that occur in the remaining functioning nephrons. when a significant number of nephrons are lost, the surviving nephrons undergo compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration in an attempt to maintain overall kidney function. initially, this adaptation is beneficial because it preserves gfr and delays the onset of symptoms. however, the increased intraglomerular pressure generated by hyperfiltration gradually damages the glomerular capillary wall. this leads to proteinuria, activation of inflammatory pathways, oxidative stress, and the release of profibrotic cytokines such as transforming growth factor-beta (tgf-β). over time, the persistent inflammatory process results in mesangial expansion, glomerulosclerosis, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. fibrosis progressively replaces functional renal tissue, leading to further nephron loss. as the number of functioning nephrons declines, the kidneys lose their ability to regulate fluid balance, electrolyte homeostasis, acid-base balance, erythropoietin production, and vitamin d metabolism. consequently, patients develop complications such as edema, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and uremia. this self-perpetuating cycle of nephron loss and fibrosis eventually culminates in end-stage kidney disease (eskd), at which point renal replacement therapy becomes necessary diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (ckd) the diagnosis of ckd is based on two fundamental criteria: 1. evidence of kidney damage, or 2. reduced kidney function (egfr \u003c60 ml/min/1.73m²) and these abnormalities must persist for at least 3 months. 1. clinical evaluation the diagnosis starts with a careful history and physical examination. history ask about: • duration of symptoms (>3 months suggests ckd) • hypertension • diabetes mellitus • recurrent urinary tract infections • hematuria • frothy urine (proteinuria) • reduced urine output • nocturia • facial puffiness or leg swelling • history of kidney stones • use of nephrotoxic drugs o nsaids o herbal medicines o aminoglycosides • family history o polycystic kidney disease o ckd • autoimmune diseases o sle o vasculitis physical examination look for: general • pallor → anemia • scratch marks → uremic pruritus • muscle wasting • weight loss vital signs • hypertension (very common) • tachypnea if acidosis fluid overload • raised jvp • bilateral pitting edema • pulmonary edema • ascites bone disease • bone tenderness • skeletal deformities neurological • confusion • peripheral neuropathy • asterixis (advanced uremia) 2. laboratory diagnosis a. serum creatinine serum creatinine is the most commonly used marker of kidney function. a raised creatinine suggests reduced gfr. however, creatinine alone does not diagnose ckd because: • it varies with muscle mass • it may be elevated in aki • elderly patients may have normal creatinine despite reduced gfr therefore: always calculate egfr. b. estimated glomerular filtration rate (egfr) egfr is the best routine measure of kidney function. it is calculated from: • serum creatinine • age • sex • race ckd is diagnosed if: egfr \u003c60 ml/min/1.73m² for ≥ 3 months or evidence of kidney damage despite normal egfr. ckd staging (kdigo) stage egfr (ml/min/1.73m²) description g1 ≥90 normal/high g2 60–89 mild reduction g3a 45–59 mild-moderate g3b 30–44 moderate-severe g4 15–29 severe g5 \u003c15 kidney failure c. urinalysis urinalysis is one of the most important investigations. look for: proteinuria suggests: • diabetic nephropathy • glomerulonephritis • fsgs • hivan hematuria suggests: • glomerulonephritis • lupus nephritis • vasculitis • stones rbc casts strongly suggest: glomerulonephritis wbc casts suggest: • interstitial nephritis • pyelonephritis d. albuminuria measure: urine albumin creatinine ratio (acr) persistent albuminuria is an early marker of ckd. kdigo albuminuria classification category acr a1 \u003c30 mg/g a2 30–300 mg/g a3 >300 mg/g e. electrolytes check: potassium hyperkalemia occurs because the kidneys cannot excrete potassium. bicarbonate low bicarbonate indicates: metabolic acidosis calcium and phosphate ckd typically causes: • ↓ calcium • ↑ phosphate parathyroid hormone (pth) usually elevated. why is pth elevated? as kidney function declines: 1. phosphate excretion decreases ↓ 2. serum phosphate rises ↓ 3. calcium falls ↓ 4. vitamin d activation decreases ↓ 5. intestinal calcium absorption falls ↓ 6. hypocalcemia stimulates parathyroid glands ↓ 7. secondary hyperparathyroidism develops. 3. imaging ultrasound kub (kidney-ureter-bladder) ultrasound is the imaging investigation of choice. typical ckd findings • small kidneys • shrunken cortex • increased cortical echogenicity • poor corticomedullary differentiation viva question which ckd conditions produce enlarged kidneys? answer 1. diabetic nephropathy 2. hiv-associated nephropathy 3. amyloidosis 4. polycystic kidney disease 5. multiple myeloma 6. acute interstitial nephritis 4. kidney biopsy kidney biopsy is not required in every patient. it is indicated when the cause is unclear or when a specific diagnosis will alter management. indications • nephrotic syndrome • rapidly progressive renal failure • unexplained proteinuria • persistent hematuria • suspected lupus nephritis • suspected vasculitis diagnostic criteria of ckd (kdigo) a patient has ckd if one or both of the following are present for ≥3 months: 1. reduced kidney function egfr \u003c60 ml/min/1.73m² or 2. evidence of kidney damage examples: • albuminuria (acr ≥30 mg/g) • urine sediment abnormalities • electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders • histological abnormalities • structural abnormalities on imaging • history of kidney transplantation differentiating ckd from aki this is a very common viva question. feature ckd aki duration >3 months hours to weeks kidney size small normal/enlarged anemia common uncommon hypocalcemia common rare hyperphosphatemia common less common osteodystrophy present absent previous creatinine elevated for months recently elevated symptoms chronic acute chronic kidney disease (ckd) section: management of ckd (mmed / davidson / kdigo style) ckd management is not simply about lowering creatinine or delaying dialysis. it is a comprehensive strategy aimed at slowing disease progression, preventing cardiovascular complications, treating metabolic abnormalities, improving quality of life, and preparing patients for renal replacement therapy when necessary. management depends on the stage of ckd, the underlying cause, and the presence of complications such as anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, or ckd-mineral bone disease. the first principle in ckd management is to identify and treat the underlying cause. a patient with diabetic nephropathy requires aggressive glycemic control, whereas a patient with lupus nephritis may require immunosuppressive therapy. similarly, obstructive uropathy should be relieved promptly to prevent further nephron loss. once the cause is identified, attention is directed toward slowing progression of ckd and managing its complications. 1. general measures all patients with ckd should receive counseling regarding lifestyle modifications. salt intake should be restricted to less than 2 g of sodium per day because excessive sodium promotes fluid retention, hypertension, and proteinuria. smoking cessation is strongly recommended because smoking accelerates decline in kidney function and increases cardiovascular risk. patients should maintain a healthy body weight and engage in regular physical activity if tolerated. nephrotoxic drugs, especially nsaids, should be avoided because they reduce renal blood flow and may precipitate aki on top of ckd. patients should also receive vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus, hepatitis b, and covid-19 when appropriate because infections contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality in ckd. 2. blood pressure control hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of ckd. poorly controlled blood pressure accelerates nephron loss and increases the risk of cardiovascular events. according to kdigo and aha guidelines: target bp • \u003c130/80 mmhg in most patients with ckd. • in patients with significant proteinuria, even stricter control may be beneficial if tolerated. ace inhibitors and arbs ace inhibitors and arbs are the preferred antihypertensive agents, especially in patients with proteinuria. these drugs reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole, thereby reducing proteinuria and slowing progression of ckd. ace inhibitors examples: • enalapril • lisinopril • ramipril enalapril dose start: • 2.5–5 mg once daily increase gradually to: • 10–20 mg daily • maximum: 40 mg/day arbs examples: • losartan • valsartan • telmisartan losartan dose start: • 25–50 mg od target: • 100 mg od side effects of ace inhibitors most examiners ask this. common side effects include: • dry cough • hyperkalemia • hypotension • dizziness • angioedema • increase in creatinine side effects of arbs • hyperkalemia • hypotension • worsening renal function importantly: arbs do not usually cause cough. caution ace inhibitors and arbs should be used cautiously in: • bilateral renal artery stenosis • severe hyperkalemia • aki • symptomatic hypotension when should acei or arb be stopped temporarily stop if: • creatinine rises >30% from baseline. • potassium >5.5–6 mmol/l. • severe dehydration. • acute illness causing aki. 3. diabetes management diabetes is the commonest cause of ckd worldwide. strict glycemic control slows progression of nephropathy and reduces cardiovascular complications. metformin metformin is often first-line therapy in type 2 diabetes. however: use according to egfr egfr recommendation >45 continue 30–45 reduce dose \u003c30 stop why stop metformin? because of the risk of: lactic acidosis especially in: • aki • sepsis • severe ckd • hypoxia sglt2 inhibitors these drugs are among the most important advances in ckd management. examples: • dapagliflozin • empagliflozin dapagliflozin dose: 10 mg once daily no titration required. benefits dapagliflozin: • reduces proteinuria • slows ckd progression • decreases hospitalization for hf • improves cardiovascular outcomes importantly: these benefits occur even in non-diabetic ckd. side effects • genital candidiasis • uti • polyuria • volume depletion • rarely: o euglycemic dka caution avoid in: • severe dehydration • active dka • type 1 diabetes (unless specialist use) 4. management of ckd anemia anemia in ckd occurs primarily because damaged kidneys cannot produce adequate erythropoietin. other contributors include iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, blood loss, and shortened red cell survival. the typical anemia is: normocytic normochromic before treating anemia: always assess: • serum ferritin • transferrin saturation (tsat) • vitamin b12 • folate iron replacement oral iron ferrous sulfate dose: 200 mg tds side effects: • constipation • black stool • epigastric discomfort iv iron examples: • iron sucrose • ferric carboxymaltose used if: • severe deficiency • oral intolerance • dialysis patients erythropoietin (epo) examiners love this. indication start epo if: hb \u003c10 g/dl after correcting: • iron deficiency • folate deficiency • b12 deficiency epoetin alpha dose: 50–100 units/kg sc three times weekly. this exact question was asked by akrabi. darbepoetin long acting. dose: 0.45 mcg/kg weekly or every 2 weeks. target hb do not normalize hb. target: 10–11.5 g/dl why? because higher hb: • increases stroke risk • increases thrombosis • increases hypertension side effects of epo • hypertension • stroke • thrombosis • headache when to transfuse? blood transfusion is not first line. indications: hb \u003c7 g/dl or hb \u003c8 g/dl with: • heart disease • severe symptoms or acute bleeding which blood? packed red blood cells not whole blood. risks of repeated transfusion • iron overload • hyperkalemia • alloimmunization • difficulty finding kidney donor later 5. ckd-mineral bone disease (ckd-mbd) this is one of nyasatu's favorite topics. as kidney function declines: • phosphate excretion decreases. • serum phosphate rises. • vitamin d activation decreases. • calcium absorption falls. • serum calcium decreases. • parathyroid hormone rises. the result is: secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy. phosphate binders calcium carbonate dose: 500–1500 mg tds take: with meals why with meals? because it binds dietary phosphate in the gut before it is absorbed. this is a common viva question. side effects • hypercalcemia • constipation • vascular calcification sevelamer dose: 800–1600 mg tds with meals. advantages: • does not cause hypercalcemia. side effects • bloating • nausea • constipation calcitriol dose: 0.25–1 mcg daily used to: • correct vitamin d deficiency • suppress pth side effects • hypercalcemia • hyperphosphatemia cinacalcet mechanism: calcimimetic. it increases sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors. ↓ suppresses pth. dose: 30 mg od can increase: 60 mg 90 mg 120 mg side effects • hypocalcemia • nausea • vomiting 6. metabolic acidosis ckd patients cannot excrete hydrogen ions adequately. result: metabolic acidosis. treat if: serum bicarbonate \u003c22 mmol/l sodium bicarbonate dose: 650–1300 mg bd–tds target: serum bicarbonate: 22–26 mmol/l side effects: • sodium overload • edema • hypertension 7. hyperkalemia very common in ckd. ecg changes earliest: peaked t waves then: • pr prolongation • wide qrs • sine wave emergency treatment if: k ≥6.5 mmol/l or ecg changes calcium gluconate 10% 10 ml iv over: 2–5 minutes. protects myocardium. insulin + dextrose 10 units regular insulin iv • 25 g dextrose. class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a preventable and treatable disease\u003cbr>characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or\u003cbr>alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 Initial Assessment\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Assess Severity\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Symptoms:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Dyspnea  o Chronic cough\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">o Sputum production  o Wheeze\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Confirm Diagnosis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Spirometry (post-bronchodilator):  FEV_1/FVC &lt; 0.70\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  FEV₁/FVC &lt; 0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assess:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (copd) is a preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases. 1. initial assessment assess severity • symptoms: o dyspnea o chronic cough o sputum production o wheeze confirm diagnosis spirometry (post-bronchodilator): fev_1/fvc \u003c 0.70 • fev₁/fvc \u003c 0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction. assess: 1. symptom burden (mmrc/cat score) 2. exacerbation history 3. comorbidities 4. oxygen saturation 2. non-pharmacological management a. smoking cessation most effective intervention. methods: • counseling • nicotine replacement therapy • varenicline • bupropion b. vaccination • influenza vaccine annually • pneumococcal vaccine • covid-19 vaccine c. pulmonary rehabilitation indicated in: • symptomatic patients • frequent exacerbations • post-hospitalization includes: • exercise training • breathing exercises • nutritional support d. nutritional support • treat malnutrition • high-protein diet e. oxygen therapy indications for long-term oxygen therapy (ltot): • pao₂ ≤55 mmhg (7.3 kpa) or • sao₂ ≤88% or • pao₂ 55–60 mmhg with: o cor pulmonale o polycythemia o right heart failure use ≥15 hours/day. 3. stable copd pharmacological treatment group a mild symptoms and low exacerbation risk. treatment: • short-acting bronchodilator as needed: o salbutamol inhaler o ipratropium inhaler or • long-acting bronchodilator (preferred) group b more symptoms but low exacerbation risk. first-line: • laba + lama examples: • salmeterol + tiotropium • formoterol + tiotropium group e frequent exacerbations. first-line: • laba + lama if eosinophils ≥300 cells/μl: • laba + lama + ics examples: • budesonide/formoterol + tiotropium common copd drugs saba • salbutamol sama • ipratropium laba • salmeterol • formoterol lama • tiotropium ics • budesonide • fluticasone 4. acute exacerbation of copd (aecopd) definition acute worsening of respiratory symptoms requiring additional therapy. common causes 1. respiratory infections 2. pneumonia 3. air pollution 4. heart failure 5. pulmonary embolism hospital management of aecopd step 1: controlled oxygen target oxygen saturation: 88–92% avoid excessive oxygen because it can worsen hypercapnia. step 2: bronchodilators nebulized salbutamol • 2.5–5 mg every 20 minutes initially plus nebulized ipratropium • 500 mcg every 4–6 hours step 3: corticosteroids prednisolone • 40 mg orally daily for 5 days or hydrocortisone iv • 100 mg every 6–8 hours if unable to take oral medication benefits: • improves fev1 • shortens recovery • reduces relapse step 4: antibiotics indications: • increased sputum volume • increased sputum purulence • increased dyspnea common options: • amoxicillin-clavulanate • azithromycin • ceftriaxone (hospitalized patients) step 5: treat precipitating cause • pneumonia • tb • heart failure • pulmonary embolism 5. non-invasive ventilation (niv) indications acute hypercapnic respiratory failure: ph \u003c 7.35 and paco_2 > 45\\ mmhg benefits: • reduces mortality • reduces need for intubation • shortens hospital stay 6. indications for intubation • respiratory arrest • severe hypoxemia despite oxygen • failure of niv • altered mental status • hemodynamic instability • severe acidosis 7. copd complications pulmonary • recurrent infections • pneumonia • pneumothorax cardiovascular • pulmonary hypertension • cor pulmonale • arrhythmias systemic • weight loss • muscle wasting • depression viva questions commonly asked 1. define copd. 2. how do you diagnose copd? 3. differentiate copd from asthma. 4. why should oxygen be given cautiously in copd? 5. what is the target oxygen saturation in copd exacerbation? 6. indications for niv in copd? 7. causes of acute exacerbation? 8. what is cor pulmonale? 9. explain the pathophysiology of co₂ retention. 10. when do you add inhaled corticosteroids? key examination pearls • copd patient + bilateral pedal edema + raised jvp → think cor pulmonale. • copd patient + sudden worsening dyspnea → think pneumothorax. • copd patient + fever and purulent sputum → think infective exacerbation. • copd patient with respiratory acidosis (high co₂) → consider niv (bipap) early.
